content: In Arctic and Antarctic ecology, a hypolith is a photosynthetic organism that resides beneath rocks in climatically extreme desert environments, such as those found on Cornwallis Island and Devon Island in the Canadian high Arctic. The community of these organisms is referred to as the hypolithon. These hypolithons are shielded from harsh ultraviolet radiation and abrasive wind scouring by the rocks under which they live. Additionally, the rocks can trap moisture, creating a more hospitable microenvironment for the organisms. The rocks that host hypoliths are typically translucent, allowing light to penetrate and support photosynthesis. Writing in Nature, ecologist Charles S. Cockell of the British Antarctic Survey and Dale Stokes described how, up until 2004, hypoliths had predominantly been found beneath quartz, one of the most common translucent rocks. However, Cockell reported that on Cornwallis Island and Devon Island, 94–95% of a random sample of 850 opaque dolomitic rocks were colonized by hypoliths. These communities were found to be dominated by cyanobacteria. The rocks selected for study were visually indistinguishable from nearby rocks and measured approximately 10 cm across. The presence of the hypolithon was evident as a greenish-colored band beneath the rocks. Cockell proposed that periglacial processes, such as those occurring during freeze-thaw cycles, may facilitate the sorting of rocks in a way that enhances light penetration around their edges. This phenomenon, which can be linked to granular material dynamics and the Brazil nut effect, may improve the conditions for hypolith colonization. Cockell further estimated that the productivity of polar hypolithons could potentially double previous estimates of the biological productivity in rocky polar desert regions, with productivity rates reaching approximately 4 g/m²/year. This finding underscores the significant ecological role of hypolithons in these extreme environments.
